Lecture 19

Residues and real integrals

We prove the residue theorem on star-shaped sets, compute the winding numbers of circles and half-discs, and define the residue at infinity. We evaluate trigonometric integrals over a period and rational integrals over the real line, and we prove the arc estimates they need, including Jordan’s estimate for the factor eikz\ee^{\iu kz}eikz.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • State the residue theorem with its hypotheses, and find the winding numbers of circles and half-disc contours around the singular points.
  • Convert an integral over a period of a rational expression in cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ and sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ into an integral around the unit circle and evaluate it by residues.
  • Evaluate a rational integral over the real line, with or without a factor eikx\ee^{\iu kx}eikx, by closing the path in the correct half-plane, and prove that the arc contributes nothing in the limit.
  • Replace a sum of residues by the residue at infinity when that is shorter.

Lecture 18 expanded a function about an isolated singular point in a Laurent series and called the coefficient of (z−z0)−1(z-z_0)^{-1}(z−z0​)−1 the residue. In this lecture we prove that the integral of a function around a closed path is 2πi2\pi\iu2πi times the sum of its residues, each counted with the winding number of the path. We then evaluate real integrals with it: integrals over a period of trigonometric expressions, and integrals of rational functions over the real line, with and without an oscillating factor eikx\ee^{\iu kx}eikx. For the line integrals the segment [−R,R][-R,R][−R,R] is closed by a semicircle whose integral must tend to zero.

19.1 The residue theorem

We recall the terms of Lecture 18. Let fff be analytic on a punctured disc 0<∣z−z0∣<r0<\abs{z-z_0}<r0<∣z−z0​∣<r. By Laurent’s theorem it is the sum of its Laurent series ∑n∈Zan(z−z0)n\sum_{n\in\Z}a_n(z-z_0)^n∑n∈Z​an​(z−z0​)n there. The part ∑n≥1a−n(z−z0)−n\sum_{n\ge1}a_{-n}(z-z_0)^{-n}∑n≥1​a−n​(z−z0​)−n is the principal part of fff at z0z_0z0​, and the residue is Res⁡z=z0f=a−1=12πi∮Cρ(z0)f(z) ⁣dz(0<ρ<r).\Res_{z=z_0}f=a_{-1}=\frac1{2\pi\iu}\oint_{C_\rho(z_0)}f(z)\dd z\qquad(0<\rho<r).Resz=z0​​f=a−1​=2πi1​∮Cρ​(z0​)​f(z)dz(0<ρ<r).

Then for every closed path CCC in UUU that passes through none of the points zkz_kzk​, ∮Cf(z) ⁣dz=2πi∑k=1mn(C,zk)Res⁡z=zkf.\oint_Cf(z)\dd z=2\pi\iu\sum_{k=1}^mn(C,z_k)\Res_{z=z_k}f .∮C​f(z)dz=2πik=1∑m​n(C,zk​)Resz=zk​​f.(19.1)

The set UUU must be star-shaped and must contain the points zkz_kzk​, where fff need not be defined. On the annulus U={1<∣z∣<3}U=\{1<\abs z<3\}U={1<∣z∣<3}, which is not star-shaped, the function 1/z1/z1/z has no singular point in UUU, yet ∮C2(0) ⁣dz/z=2πi\oint_{C_2(0)}\dd z/z=2\pi\iu∮C2​(0)​dz/z=2πi. Its residue lies at 0∉U0\notin U0∈/U.

Each singular point counts with the winding number of the path around it. For a circle Lecture 17 computed these numbers: Cr(z0)C_r(z_0)Cr​(z0​) winds once around every point of Br(z0)B_r(z_0)Br​(z0​) and zero times around every point outside B‾r(z0)\overline B_r(z_0)Br​(z0​). A disc and the plane are star-shaped, so the theorem gives the following form.

19.2 The point at infinity

A large circle encloses all singular points of a function with finitely many of them. Its integral is then decided by the behaviour of the function for large ∣z∣\abs z∣z∣. We add a point ∞\infty∞ to the plane and obtain the extended plane C∪{∞}\C\cup\{\infty\}C∪{∞}. The substitution z=1/wz=1/wz=1/w maps the set ∣z∣>R0\abs z>R_0∣z∣>R0​ onto the punctured disc 0<∣w∣<1/R00<\abs w<1/R_00<∣w∣<1/R0​, and the point ∞\infty∞ corresponds to w=0w=0w=0.

Let fff be analytic on ∣z∣>R0\abs z>R_0∣z∣>R0​. Then g(w)=f(1/w)g(w)=f(1/w)g(w)=f(1/w) is analytic on 0<∣w∣<1/R00<\abs w<1/R_00<∣w∣<1/R0​, so w=0w=0w=0 is an isolated singular point of ggg. We say that fff has a removable singularity, a pole of order mmm or an essential singularity at ∞\infty∞ when ggg has one at 000. For example, a polynomial of degree m≥1m\ge1m≥1 has a pole of order mmm at ∞\infty∞, the function ez\ee^zez has an essential singularity there, and 1/z1/z1/z has a removable one, since g(w)=wg(w)=wg(w)=w.

Definition 19.4 (Residue at infinity). Let fff be analytic on ∣z∣>R0\abs z>R_0∣z∣>R0​, with the Laurent series ∑n∈Zanzn\sum_{n\in\Z}a_nz^n∑n∈Z​an​zn there. The residue of fff at infinity is Res⁡z=∞f=−a−1=−12πi∮Cρ(0)f(z) ⁣dz(ρ>R0).\Res_{z=\infty}f=-a_{-1}=-\frac1{2\pi\iu}\oint_{C_\rho(0)}f(z)\dd z\qquad(\rho>R_0).Resz=∞​f=−a−1​=−2πi1​∮Cρ​(0)​f(z)dz(ρ>R0​).(19.5)

The two expressions agree by Laurent’s theorem with r1=R0r_1=R_0r1​=R0​ and r2=∞r_2=\inftyr2​=∞, and they do not depend on ρ\rhoρ. The minus sign comes from the orientation. The circle Cρ(0)C_\rho(0)Cρ​(0) traversed clockwise keeps the set ∣z∣>ρ\abs z>\rho∣z∣>ρ, which surrounds ∞\infty∞, on its left. So the clockwise direction is the positive orientation around ∞\infty∞, and (19.5) is the integral in that direction divided by 2πi2\pi\iu2πi, as for a finite point. Ablowitz and Fokas (§4.1) use the opposite sign.

∣Res⁡z=∞f∣≤12π⋅Kρ2⋅2πρ=Kρ,\abs{\Res_{z=\infty}f}\le\frac1{2\pi}\cdot\frac K{\rho^2}\cdot2\pi\rho=\frac K\rho ,∣Resz=∞​f∣≤2π1​⋅ρ2K​⋅2πρ=ρK​,(19.6)

Proposition 19.6 (Sum of all residues). Let fff be analytic on C\CC except at finitely many points z1,…,zmz_1,\ldots,z_mz1​,…,zm​. Then ∑k=1mRes⁡z=zkf+Res⁡z=∞f=0.\sum_{k=1}^m\Res_{z=z_k}f+\Res_{z=\infty}f=0 .k=1∑m​Resz=zk​​f+Resz=∞​f=0.

19.4 Rational integrals over the real line

To evaluate ∫−∞∞P(x)/Q(x) ⁣dx\int_{-\infty}^\infty P(x)/Q(x)\dd x∫−∞∞​P(x)/Q(x)dx we close the segment [−R,R][-R,R][−R,R] with the arc ARA_RAR​ and let R→∞R\to\inftyR→∞. Two facts must be shown. The integral over ARA_RAR​ must tend to zero, and the integrals over [−R,R][-R,R][−R,R] must tend to the improper integral. The second fact needs care. An improper integral over the line requires both limits, at +∞+\infty+∞ and at −∞-\infty−∞, separately (GM 27), but the contour gives only the symmetric integral ∫−RR\int_{-R}^R∫−RR​. For x/(x2+1)x/(x^2+1)x/(x2+1) the symmetric integral is 000 for every RRR, because the integrand is odd, while ∫0Rx ⁣dx/(x2+1)=12ln⁡(R2+1)\int_0^R x\dd x/(x^2+1)=\frac12\ln(R^2+1)∫0R​xdx/(x2+1)=21​ln(R2+1) tends to infinity. So the improper integral of x/(x2+1)x/(x^2+1)x/(x2+1) diverges, although its symmetric limit exists.

Both facts follow from bounds on polynomials for large ∣z∣\abs z∣z∣, as in the proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra in Lecture 17.

19.5 Oscillating factors and Jordan’s estimate

The Fourier integrals of Lectures 23, 24 and 28 contain a factor eikx\ee^{\iu kx}eikx with a real wave number kkk, or eiωt\ee^{\iu\omega t}eiωt with a real frequency ω\omegaω. For k>0k>0k>0 and z=x+iyz=x+\iu yz=x+iy we have ∣eikz∣=e−ky\abs{\ee^{\iu kz}}=\ee^{-ky}​eikz​=e−ky, which is at most 111 in the upper half-plane and decreases as yyy grows. When P/QP/QP/Q decays only like 1/∣x∣1/\abs x1/∣x∣, the length estimate on ARA_RAR​ gives a bounded quantity but not one that tends to zero. Jordan’s estimate uses the decay of eikz\ee^{\iu kz}eikz away from the real axis.

Lemma 19.14 (Jordan’s estimate). Let k>0k>0k>0 and R>0R>0R>0, and let ggg be continuous on the arc ARA_RAR​ with ∣g∣≤M\abs g\le M∣g∣≤M there. Then ∣∫AReikzg(z) ⁣dz∣≤πMk.\abs{\int_{A_R}\ee^{\iu kz}g(z)\dd z}\le\frac{\pi M}k .​∫AR​​eikzg(z)dz​≤kπM​.(19.13)

Proposition 19.15 (Rational integrals with an oscillating factor). Let PPP and QQQ be polynomials with deg⁡Q≥deg⁡P+1\deg Q\ge\deg P+1degQ≥degP+1, let Q(x)≠0Q(x)\ne0Q(x)=0 for every real xxx, and let k≠0k\ne0k=0 be real. By Lemma 19.10, ∣h(x)∣≤K/∣x∣\abs{h(x)}\le K/\abs x∣h(x)∣≤K/∣x∣ for ∣x∣≥RQ\abs x\ge R_Q∣x∣≥RQ​, so h(x)→0h(x)\to0h(x)→0 as ∣x∣→∞\abs x\to\infty∣x∣→∞. Example 19.16 (The Lorentzian). Let a>0a>0a>0 and k∈Rk\in\Rk∈R. ∫−∞∞cos⁡(kx)x2+a2 ⁣dx=πa e−∣k∣a.\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{\cos(kx)}{x^2+a^2}\dd x=\frac\pi a\,\ee^{-\abs k a}.∫−∞∞​x2+a2cos(kx)​dx=aπ​e−∣k∣a.(19.17)

Example 19.17 (An integral that needs Jordan’s estimate). Let a>0a>0a>0 and k>0k>0k>0. The arc estimate shows why Jordan’s estimate is needed. On ARA_RAR​ with R>aR>aR>a we have ∣h∣≤R/(R2−a2)\abs h\le R/(R^2-a^2)∣h∣≤R/(R2−a2). As k→0+k\to0^+k→0+ the value tends to π\piπ, but at k=0k=0k=0 the integrand is 000, and for k<0k<0k<0 the integral is −πeka-\pi\ee^{ka}−πeka, because sin⁡\sinsin is odd. The integral is discontinuous at k=0k=0k=0, so a limit k→0k\to0k→0 cannot be taken under the integral sign here. ◃

∫−∞∞xsin⁡(kx)x2+a2 ⁣dx=πe−ka.\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{x\sin(kx)}{x^2+a^2}\dd x=\pi\ee^{-ka}.∫−∞∞​x2+a2xsin(kx)​dx=πe−ka.(19.18)

Jordan’s estimate is a sufficient bound for one situation: a semicircular arc and an integrand eikzg(z)\ee^{\iu kz}g(z)eikzg(z) with max⁡AR∣g∣→0\max_{A_R}\abs g\to0maxAR​​∣g∣→0. It does not permit closing a contour in general. The Bromwich inversion of Lecture 27 integrates estF(s)\ee^{st}F(s)estF(s) along a vertical line in the plane of the Laplace variable sss. Closing that path needs its own check of the growth of FFF on the added arcs, and Lecture 27 states and checks it for each class of transforms FFF it uses.

Summary

The residue theorem turns a closed contour integral into a sum of residues weighted by winding numbers. Real integrals over a period become integrals around the unit circle. Real integrals over the line are closed by a semicircle in the half-plane where the integrand decays. The arc integral tends to zero by the length estimate or, with a factor eikz\ee^{\iu kz}eikz, by Jordan’s estimate.

  • Residue theorem: ∮Cf ⁣dz=2πi∑kn(C,zk)Res⁡z=zkf\oint_Cf\dd z=2\pi\iu\sum_kn(C,z_k)\Res_{z=z_k}f∮C​fdz=2πi∑k​n(C,zk​)Resz=zk​​f for fff analytic on a star-shaped open set UUU except at z1,…,zm∈Uz_1,\ldots,z_m\in Uz1​,…,zm​∈U and a closed path CCC in UUU avoiding them.

  • Winding numbers: Cr(z0)C_r(z_0)Cr​(z0​) and ∂DR\partial D_R∂DR​ wind once around the points of the open disc and the open upper half-disc; the clockwise path −∂DR−-\partial D_R^-−∂DR−​ winds −1-1−1 times around the points of the open lower half-disc.

  • Infinity: Res⁡z=∞f=−a−1=−Res⁡w=0f(1/w)/w2\Res_{z=\infty}f=-a_{-1}=-\Res_{w=0}f(1/w)/w^2Resz=∞​f=−a−1​=−Resw=0​f(1/w)/w2; for fff analytic on C\CC except at finitely many points, the residue at infinity and all finite residues add up to zero; Res⁡z=∞f=0\Res_{z=\infty}f=0Resz=∞​f=0 when ∣f∣≤K/∣z∣2\abs f\le K/\abs z^2∣f∣≤K/∣z∣2 for large ∣z∣\abs z∣z∣.

  • Real integrals: over a period with z=eiθz=\ee^{\iu\theta}z=eiθ; ∫RP/Q ⁣dx=2πi∑Im⁡zj>0Res⁡P/Q\int_{\R}P/Q\dd x=2\pi\iu\sum_{\Im z_j>0}\Res P/Q∫R​P/Qdx=2πi∑Imzj​>0​ResP/Q when deg⁡Q≥deg⁡P+2\deg Q\ge\deg P+2degQ≥degP+2 and QQQ has no real zero; with eikx\ee^{\iu kx}eikx, k>0k>0k>0, the same formula holds for deg⁡Q≥deg⁡P+1\deg Q\ge\deg P+1degQ≥degP+1 by Jordan’s estimate, and k<0k<0k<0 closes below with a minus sign.

Lecture 20 lets the path pass singular points on the real axis on small semicircles, compares ordinary and principal-value integrals, and integrates along the two banks of a branch cut.

Reading: M. J. Ablowitz and A. S. Stein and R. Shakarchi, Complex Analysis, Chapter 3, §2 (the residue formula and its examples).
